body.heading: A garden for children
paragraphs: In 1837, the German educator Friedrich Froebel opened a school for young children unlike any before it: no desks in rows, no rote lessons, but songs, gardens, and sets of simple wooden shapes — balls, cubes, cylinders — that he called “gifts”. He named it a kindergarten: a garden where children grow as plants do, by nature, with a gardener's care.

Froebel's scandalous idea was that play is not the opposite of learning but its engine. Through the gifts, children explored shape, number, balance and symmetry with their hands long before they met them in books.

body.heading: What play teaches
paragraphs: Modern research keeps agreeing with him. Block play rehearses geometry and engineering; pretend play practises language, empathy and self-control — a child staying “in role” as a shopkeeper is exercising willpower as real as any worksheet's. Games with rules teach fairness and losing gracefully, which no lecture has ever managed.

None of this makes play soft. Watch a child determined to build a tower taller than themselves and you will see concentration, hypothesis-testing (“what if the big block goes on top?”) and resilience through collapse — a complete scientific method, in miniature, before lunch.

body.heading: Try it: the ten-minute laboratory
paragraphs: Give a child (or yourself) ten plain objects — blocks, boxes, cups — and one challenge: build something that can hold a book, or a bridge a toy car can cross. No instructions, no model to copy. Then ask the builder to explain what they discovered.
The explaining is where the learning doubles. Teaching a discovery to someone else is the oldest study technique in the world — and it works at every age, including yours.

takeaway: Froebel called play “the highest expression of human development” in childhood — two centuries later, the blocks are still teaching.
